records.quote: Flames had enveloped the whole house with appalling swiftness, and now the great mass was etched against the shadowed sky, a crimson inferno.
records.paraphrase: The house is rapidly consumed by fire into a blazing inferno.

records.quote: they all say that in the intervening years he seems not to have aged perceptibly. When he came here he looked just as he does now--or did, up to the moment of his death--of the appearance of a man about fifty.
records.paraphrase: Grimlan is reported to have not aged over twenty years, appearing about fifty throughout.

records.quote: he knew Grimlan when a very young man studying in Berlin, fifty years ago, and he expressed astonishment that the old man was still living; for he said at that time Grimlan seemed to be about fifty years of age.
records.paraphrase: An elderly professor recalls Grimlan looking fifty fifty years earlier, implying he has not aged.

records.quote: for a price maye he gain hys heartes desire, ryches & knowledge beyond countinge & lyffe beyond mortal span even two hundred & fiftie yeares.
records.paraphrase: The incantation describes a bargain granting an unnaturally extended lifespan of 250 years.

records.quote: I had been appalled at the writhings, howlings and yammerings of the wretch, who had groveled on the earth like a wounded snake, gibbering terrible curses and black blasphemies until his voice broke in a wordless screaming which spattered his lips with foam.
records.paraphrase: The narrator recalls being horrified by witnessing Grimlan's violent seizure.

records.quote: John Grymlann, borne, March 10, 1630." And then we both cried out. Under this entry was freshly written, in a strange scrawling hand, "Died, March 10, 1930.
records.paraphrase: A genealogy record dates Grimlan's birth to 1630 and his death to 1930, spanning three centuries.

records.quote: beinge of rite mynd & fiftie years of age this yeare of 1680, A.D.
records.paraphrase: Grimlan's own written incantation states he was fifty years old in 1680.

records.quote: above the holocaust hovered a gigantic black shadow like a monstrous bat, and from its dark clutch dangled a small white thing, like the body of a man, dangling limply.
records.paraphrase: A huge bat-like shadow carries off a man-shaped body above the burning house.

records.quote: Professor Von Boehnk is past eighty himself, and liable to the errors of extreme age. He confused this man with another." Yet as I spoke, my flesh crawled unpleasantly and the hairs on my neck prickled.
records.paraphrase: The narrator rationalizes the aging anomaly while physically recoiling in dread.

records.quote: I have been at pains to inquire about him discreetly," said Conrad. "He has lived here--with the exception of mysterious absences often for months at a time--for twenty years.
records.paraphrase: Conrad describes systematically investigating Grimlan's history by questioning villagers.

records.quote: Old John doubtless fell heir to some ingrown weakness brought on by some loathsome disease, which was his heritage from perhaps a remote ancestor--such things occasionally happen.
records.paraphrase: Conrad offers a medical, hereditary-disease explanation for Grimlan's condition.

records.quote: The last candle went out suddenly and a ghastly unhuman cry that came not from my lips or from Conrad's burst unbearably forth.
records.paraphrase: When the final candle goes out, an inhuman cry and chaos erupt in the dark room.

records.quote: It is quite possible that he was infected with some obscure malady in his wanderings. There are still many unclassified diseases in Africa and the Orient.
records.paraphrase: Conrad proposes that Grimlan caught an unclassified tropical disease during his travels.

records.quote: showed us the black ebony table--empty! The doors and windows were locked as they had been, but the oriental was gone--and so was the corpse of John Grimlan.
records.paraphrase: The corpse and the oriental visitor vanish from a still-locked room.

records.quote: Soul and body he sold to Malik Tous, who is Satan, two hundred and fifty years ago! This was the night of payment--and my God--look!
records.paraphrase: Conrad cries out interpreting the events as the collection of a 250-year-old demonic bargain.

criteria.rationale: The only science-flavored content is Conrad's speculative disease/hereditary-taint rationalization, which is offered and then discarded as inadequate. There is no scientific fact, theory, discovery, or natural process materially represented; the story is supernatural/occult in framing.
No device, engineered system, or invention materially affects the setting or outcome. Candles, parchment, and an incantation are ritual/occult objects, not technology or invention in the SF sense.

Grimlan's 300-year lifespan (1630-1930) and unaging appearance constitute temporal displacement of a sort, but it is framed as a supernatural/Faustian bargain rather than speculative future, remote past, or mechanical time travel, so the reading is plausible but interpretively uncertain.

The story develops consequences from an identifiable premise (a bargain for a 250-year extended life), tracing it to the fated night of payment. However, the premise is a supernatural pact rather than a scientific/technological one, so extrapolation is present in structure but uncertain in kind.

Conrad's discreet inquiries and the narrator's rationalizations are generic investigation and denial, not systematic hypothesis-testing, measurement, or evidential revision that drives understanding. The men ultimately accept a supernatural explanation, not a methodically derived one.

References to the dead city of Koth, the Elder Ones, and an otherworldly visitor (the oriental figure/bat-shadow entity that appears and vanishes from a locked room) evoke nonordinary cosmic environments and a visitor from beyond, but these are supernatural/demonic rather than clearly cosmic-SF, leaving materiality and interpretation uncertain.

The climax features the house consumed by a crimson inferno that collapses in an earth-shaking roar, an actual large-scale destructive conflagration causally central to the story's resolution and Grimlan's claiming.

candidates.description: The core premise that John Grimlan, born in 1630, extended his life beyond mortal span to 250 years through a supernatural bargain with Malik Tous (Satan)/the Elder Ones of dead Koth, whose payment comes due at the appointed hour, culminating in the fiend claiming his soul and body.

novelty.rationale: The unnatural longevity and the fiend's claiming of the body do represent a world-altering difference from the empirical norm, but the operative account is explicitly a soul-selling pact with Satan (Malik Tous, 'the veritable Satan') and 'the Fiend claiming his own.' This is a supernatural/theological difference, not a totalizing cognitive one. Suvin's novum requires estrangement grounded in a nonsupernatural, immanent logic; here the difference is framed as literal devil-worship, damnation, and demonic collection, placing it in the register of the marvelous/gothic-horror rather than science-fictional novelty.

cognitive_validation.rationale: Although the narrator (Kirowan) and Conrad offer rationalist counter-explanations (hereditary disease, unclassified tropical maladies, aged professor's error, a madman's hoax) and Conrad conducts discreet inquiry, these naturalistic accounts are systematically overturned by the narrative. The final, sanctioned explanation is explicitly supernatural: a pact with Satan, an incantation invoking Ahriman/Beelzebub/Malik Tous, and a demonic bat-shadow bearing off the corpse. There is no coherent, immanent, nonsupernatural system underwriting the phenomenon; it rests on 'There is no god but evil' and 'the Fiend claimed his own.' The account is therefore not cognitively validated in Suvin's sense.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The bargain and its due-date payment govern the entire narrative logic: Grimlan's unaging appearance, his terror-filled death, the sealed instructions, the midnight ritual over the corpse, the arrival of the oriental agent, the vanishing of body and stranger from a locked room, and the final immolation with the bat-shadow bearing the body away. Every major event flows from and toward the 250-year contract's fulfillment, making it clearly central rather than incidental.

estrangement.rationale: Reader-facing contrast is sharpest at the genealogy entry (born 1630, died 1930) and Grimlan's own incantation dating himself to fifty years of age in 1680, jarring against the empirical norm of a mortal lifespan. Storyworld consequences include the impossible disappearance from a locked room, the fire, and the bat-shape carrying off a man-sized body. Character reactions (Kirowan's crawling flesh, Conrad's climactic cry naming the 250-year sale to Satan) register the estrangement, though such reaction is not required for the assessment.
